newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin turns from Chechen deal to NATO talks.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin turns from Chechen deal to NATO talks.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, boosted by a treaty aimed at formally ending the bloody war in Chechnya, turns his attention on Tuesday to an elusive long-term pact with Russian's Cold War foe NATO.
As he prepared for a new round of talks with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana, Yeltsin began a round of telephone diplomacy with Western leaders by calling French President Jacques Chirac.

Chirac hopes to host the signing of a treaty in Paris on May 27. Officials say it may give Russia security guarantees, such as assurances that the West will not advance nuclear arms into new member states, and a say in NATO decision-making.

But both Moscow, bitterly opposed to NATO's plans to admit former Soviet satellites in Eastern Europe, and NATO, adamant it will not appease Russia to the detriment of new members like Poland, have said they cannot be certain of meeting that deadline.

Solana is due to hold new negotiations with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Tuesday evening. As in the past, neither side plans to brief reporters and it seems unlikely there will be dramatic announcements, whatever progress is made.
Some Kremlin sources, as well as Western insiders, have said Yeltsin has made up his mind to sign a deal this month.
Analysts say that may prompt the Russian leader to gloss over differences to allow for a public show of diplomatic success.

The vaguely-worded peace treaty Yeltsin signed with Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov on Monday was seen as an example of the Kremlin leader's determination to end a flagging negotiating process with a document setting out common views but risking skirting over the nub of the dispute.
Yeltsin said the acccord consisted of only one point: "A peace treaty has been signed. This is the gist of it."
As provided by the Kremlin, there were three points:
-- That Russia and the breakaway Moslem region would never again resort to the violence that culminated in a 21-month war and tens of thousands of deaths up to August 1996.
-- That relations would follow "norms of international law".
-- That the treaty would be the basis for future accords.
Both leaders, speaking after the signing in the Kremlin, said the document marked the end of four centuries of conflict between Moscow and the north Caucasus people.
"We have signed a peace deal of historic dimensions, putting a full stop to 400 years of history," Yeltsin said.

Yet it was not clear how far the two sides had actually settled the principle sticking point in negotiations that followed last August's ceasefire -- Russia's refusal to grant Chechnya full sovereign independence under international law.

Despite the reference to relations in accordance with international law, Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky stressed in an interview with Interfax news agency that Yeltsin had no intention of letting Chechnya secede from Russia.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said the treaty "does not address the question of Chechnya's status" and recalled that under the ceasefire terms, that was put off for five years, until 2001.

Several other ethnic regions in Russia have specific accords allowing them considerable autonomy from Moscow and even the possibility of forging economic ties abroad. But any move to seek separate political recognition is anathema to Moscow.

In Chechnya's case, Moscow seemed anxious to provide the more moderate Maskhadov with something he could use to head off more hardline elements in the heavily-armed and impoverished region. Maskhadov also won much needed economic accords.
The Chechen leader praised Yeltsin's statesmanship and pledged to stamp out "terrorists" in Chechnya -- an echo of the words the Kremlin used when it first attacked the separatists.
As with any NATO deal, the test of the Chechen treaty will be whether the goodwill on display on Monday can be maintained.
